newsitem.title: USA: US fertilizer supplies taxed by corn planting rush.
newsitem.headline: US fertilizer supplies taxed by corn planting rush.

text.p: Farmers rushing to plant corn at the earliest possible date to beat spring rains have drawn down local fertilizer supplies, industry sources said.

"There have been spot shortages of anhydrous ammonia in southern Nebraska because it is going on so fast," said Leon Stonecipher, a marketing director for Farmland Industries, a major agricultural cooperative.
Farmers also are adding more fertilizer this spring to compensate for a late corn harvest last fall that did not allow time to add normal fertilizer applications.
Shipping delays on the Mississippi, Missouri and Arkansas Rivers have slowed the arrival of fertilizers at key distribution centers in Catoosa, Okla., and Kansas City, Mo.
"In the Midwest there are shortages. We have very low supplies," said a anhydrous ammonia supplier. Barge loading and shipping problems slowed anhydrous movement to the Midwest, the supplier said.

Prices for granular fertilizer diammonium phosphate, basis Kansas City, have risen about $5 per ton since last week to $205 to $208 per ton. Cash dealers said strong demand coupled with shipping delays could add another $5 to prices next week.
"We are struggling to keep inventories here (Kansas City) on urea and phosphates," Stonecipher said.
Urea is a granular fertilizer that adds nitrogen to corn fields.
Warehouse supplies ran low this winter because dealers were slow to build inventory following a disappointing fall sales season, grain dealers said.

"Production is available, it just can't get to where it needs to get to," said an Oklahoma dealer. "There are a lot of people who have yet to buy, and if they are short they are going to pay whatever they have to."

The anhydrous ammonia supplier said Midwest prices have been steady from $245 to $250 per ton but could move higher if demand continues. But rain forecast for this weekend could halt planting in much of the Midwest, which could quickly ease fertilizer supply shortages, he said.
"Weather would slow things down a lot and that would help suppliers get product in place," said the Oklahoma dealer.
Fieldwork is under way from Nebraska to Indiana, with scattered corn planting in Nebraska, Iowa and Illinois.

Abundant rain the past two years delayed spring planting in the Midwest, and this year farmers appear willing to risk a late blast of cold weather by planting corn at the earliest opportunity, grain officials said.

"Last week I heard of a couple of guys planting corn already," said Indiana Farm Bureau market economist Joe Miller. "That gives you an idea of how edgy they are to get out in the fields. We should see the crop get planted very, very early."
Several fertilizer dealers said early fertilizer sales support USDA's corn and soybean acreage estimates.
On March 31, USDA estimated corn plantings at 81.416 million acres versus 79.487 million a year ago and soybean acreage at 68.80 million versus 64.205 million last year.
